candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the agent name in the /computer/<name>/... URL. No special value or token is needed: getJnlpMac derives the secret from the requested agent name under the server-held SLAVE_SECRET key. The resulting value is returned directly by the getter.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I verified that the root Jenkins target gate checks only READ, that ComputerSet.getDynamic does not perform a per-computer check, and that SlaveComputer.getJnlpMac has no checkPermission/StaplerProxy guard. The plaintext JNLP endpoint passes CONNECT into EncryptedSlaveAgentJnlpFile, so the intended permission exists, but the getter bypasses that endpoint. DefaultJnlpSlaveReceiver rejects a duplicate connection when an agent is already connected unless the connection cookie matches, so impersonation is conditional on agent availability; it does not prevent disclosure of the reusable secret. I also considered that the snapshot omits Jelly views and runtime execution, so direct getter serialization remains unconfirmed.
candidates.impact: A user with only Overall/Read can obtain a per-agent authentication secret and can attempt JNLP agent impersonation, potentially running jobs as that agent, reading its workspace/artifacts and build-bound credentials, or reaching the controller depending on master-to-agent security configuration. The same authorization gap can disclose JVM system properties and process environment variables, which commonly contain credentials, proxy settings, tokens, and filesystem paths.
candidates.prerequisites: Jenkins security is enabled and the attacker has an account with Overall/Read (or anonymous READ is granted). For the strongest impact, at least one JNLP-capable agent is configured, the JNLP transport is reachable, and the target agent is offline or otherwise not holding the connection slot when the attacker attempts to use the disclosed secret. No runtime exploit was attempted.
candidates.root_cause: ComputerSet resolves a requested Computer without a computer-specific authorization check, and Computer/SlaveComputer expose sensitive state through public JavaBean getters that have no checkPermission call. Jenkins.getTarget only enforces Overall/Read for these paths. SlaveComputer.getJnlpMac() therefore returns the same HMAC-derived agent secret used by JnlpAgentReceiver to authenticate JNLP connections; the same class pattern also exposes JVM system properties, environment variables, agent logs, and thread dumps.
candidates.title: Missing authorization on Computer getters exposes the JNLP agent secret and sensitive diagnostics
candidates.trace: 1) Jenkins.getTarget() requires only Jenkins.READ for ordinary /computer/... paths. 2) ComputerSet.getDynamic() returns the requested Computer without checking Computer.CONNECT, Computer.CONFIGURE, or another computer-scoped permission. 3) Stapler exposes public getters; SlaveComputer.getJnlpMac() has no permission check and returns JnlpSlaveAgentProtocol.SLAVE_SECRET.mac(agentName). 4) JnlpAgentReceiver.JnlpAgentDatabase.getSecretOf() uses the identical SLAVE_SECRET.mac(clientName) value as the JNLP client secret, so disclosure of the getter result is disclosure of the credential used by the JNLP receiver. 5) The same unguarded getter pattern exposes Computer.getSystemProperties()/getEnvironment() and agent log/thread-dump data; Computer.getLogText() elsewhere explicitly checks CONNECT, showing that sensitive Computer access is expected to be gated. 6) If an agent slot is available, the disclosed secret permits an attacker to authenticate a rogue agent connection and act under that agent identity, subject to remoting security settings.
candidates.unverified: No execution or runtime request was performed. Stapler getter routing and scalar/collection rendering were inferred from the public-getter convention (for example getApi endpoints) rather than observed. The snapshot contains no Jelly views or tests, so any view-level permission checks or separate restrictions cannot be inspected. JNLP agent impersonation additionally depends on the JNLP port/protocol being enabled, the target agent being offline or reconnectable, and the configured master-to-agent security policy.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-862 Missing Authorization / improper access control

coverage_summary: Source scope reports 9,725 visible files and the relation index reports complete coverage of all 9,725 source files. I inspected the main Java routing and authorization paths around Jenkins, ComputerSet, Computer/SlaveComputer, CLI commands, CSRF, XStream class filtering, agent/JNLP handling, FilePath archive extraction, and directory/file-serving code. I did not line-by-line review all 1,034 core Java files or the large resource/localization set, and the snapshot contains no tests or Jelly views, which limits verification of view-level authorization.
limitations: Static source review only; no code, tests, server, or exploit payloads were executed.
The snapshot omits tests and Jelly view files, so presentation-layer permission checks and direct Stapler rendering behavior could not be verified.
Stapler routing of JavaBean getters and scalar/collection rendering was inferred from source conventions, not runtime-confirmed.
JNLP agent impersonation depends on JNLP availability, agent connection state, and master-to-agent security configuration.
The relation index is syntactic/navigation-only and was not treated as proof of data flow or reachability.
Coverage was broad and targeted rather than exhaustive; resource and localization files were not reviewed line by line.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal in FilePath.unzip/readFromTar entry extraction
rejected_leads.reason: Both extractors construct destination files directly from entry names without canonical containment checks. However, this snapshot does not show a direct low-privilege core HTTP path that extracts an attacker-supplied archive; the likely callers are plugins, administrators, or internally generated snapshots, so the attacker-to-sink path was not sufficiently established for the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SoloFilePathFilter symlink bypass in master-to-agent access control
rejected_leads.reason: The filter normalizes lexically rather than resolving symlink targets. Exploitation appears to require a compromised agent and active master-to-agent file filtering, and I could not establish the required symlink race/configuration from this source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: Open redirect via backslash forms in Util.isSafeToRedirectTo
rejected_leads.reason: The check rejects absolute URIs and leading // but not leading backslashes. Browser normalization and the exact redirect response behavior were not verified, and the impact is lower than the authorization issue.
The header is AES-encrypted with a server-held key and timestamp-checked. No practical attacker-controlled path to produce a valid encrypted payload was established, so this remains speculative.

summary: Reviewed the Jenkins core snapshot as a source-level access-control and file-handling review. I submit one candidate: public Computer/SlaveComputer getters are Stapler-addressable but lack object-level permission checks, most critically exposing the per-agent JNLP HMAC secret and, through the same pattern, JVM system properties/environment diagnostics to any user with Overall/Read. Other suspicious areas were considered but not promoted because their attacker path was indirect or unverified.
